utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the witness makes the declaration, may I say that we will allow the video to be referred to during the course of the witness's evidence. If, at a later stage, there's an argument for exclusion, we will consider it, but for the moment, it will be admitted. Yes, if the witness would like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Full name, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: My name is John Bartlett Allcock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, your report contains --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, your report contains at Roman pages I and II notes about yourself and notes about some of your publications. I don't intend to run through that in any detail but to amplify it simply to this extent: You set out your principal publications, but what is your first special interest in Yugoslavia reflected by a publication of papers and one thing and another?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think that would be about 1977, yes. My first area of interest in Yugoslav affairs was in the development of Yugoslav agriculture, and I published a chapter in "A Historical Geography of the Balkans," edited by Frank Carter, that was published, I think, in 1977. That would be the first major publication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a speaker of the language?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having acquired it when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Over the years, my first visit to the former Yugoslavia was the Easter of 1967, and the University of Bradford shortly acquired after that the capacity to teach the language, so I pursued courses at Brantford. But I think my first scholarship in Yugoslavia through the British Council was, I believe, in 1970. So from that point onward, I began to attend courses at various centres in the country itself, so intermittently since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Visiting the former Yugoslavia with what approximate frequency?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Very variable, actually. In the early days, I had fewer family and university obligations so was able to spend quite long periods of time there, with scholarships extending over several months, two or three months at a time. There's rarely been a year since 1967 when I have not visited the country. But for lengths of time varying from a week to three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the publications that you cite as being your principal publications, are you also a contributor to something called the Annual Register of World Events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct. Perhaps I should have included this in the list of publications which I mentioned here. The Annual Register is quite a useful reference source which appears each year with entries for every country in the world, and I think for the past ten years, I have been the contributor, first of all, relating to Yugoslavia, but subsequently to the states which have emerged from the former Yugoslav Federation. I think the importance of those publications are that they suggest that I have a familiarity with the region which extends beyond simply my own narrow profession of sociology, because one has to review in those publications also the primary political and economic developments on a fairly broad front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Roman II, you set out forthcoming a book on Yugoslavia at the time of typing it up. It was to be called "Historical Sociology". The present position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I'm delighted to say that the script has been very well received to the publisher who immediately sent it on to Columbia University Press, and it looks as if there will be a simultaneous publication of an American edition. We will be using a slightly different title, "Explaining Yugoslavia," but there were some very warm reports, indeed, from the publishers' readers, so that is certainly going to be going ahead very shortly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the first overall, you say, sociological characterisation of the long-term historical development of Yugoslav society?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Obviously, political scientists, such as Denison Rousinow, have for a long time been producing accounts of the country. My former colleague, Fred Singleton, has made his contributions as a geographer. This is the first attempt by a sociologist to produce a broad, overall characterisation of Yugoslavia and its historical development.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please ask the witness to speak more slowly because of the interpretation? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The previous witness, Dr. Donia, first of all, did you, before becoming involved in this case, know of him; just "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, before becoming to be involved in this case, know him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: We met briefly at a conference, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, I'd used both of his major books, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to express a view on your own view of him as an academic, or however you would describe him, and are you able to express a view on how he is regarded in the academic community?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I have high regard for him as a historian, and I think that view would be shared by professional colleagues too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, the film that we've all recently seen, it's not a film that's referred to in your report in any way, was it a film that you had in mind to refer to when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think this is something of an oversight on my part, in that having been asked to write a report, my mind was rather fixed on the production of printed evidence. If I'd used my imagination a little bit earlier, I might have suggested to the Court sooner. It does fit in admirably with the kinds of argument that I've tried to develop in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of us have seen it comparatively recently. In short, what is its significance so far as the conclusions you draw are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Its significance with respect to the argument I've tried to develop in my report is simply twofold. First of all, I lay quite a strong emphasis on the idea that hostility between different ethnic groups in the region is not something which is deeply rooted and pervasive in the population of the area but is something which has been fostered more recently as a consequence of the conflict, rather than as its precondition. I think the film shows that very clearly, shows the way in which neighbours do relate to each other, in an easy, friendly manner, in the ordinary course of their lives. But, secondly, it illustrates very clearly the way in which such difficulties as there are in their relationships intrude into the village by forces coming from the outside, rather than hostility developing spontaneously between the population of that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report contains several charts and maps, and I want your brief explanation on them to ensure that they are properly understood, and so far as the colour ones, that the Court has the advantage of colour as opposed to black and white ones and is able to interpret them. First, in your report at page 25, there's the first of three pages of statistics summarised that we must be sure we understand.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 24 itself, we have the ethnic structure of the population of Yugoslavia in 1991, and the table below, the ethnic structure of the population of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the same year. Significance or interpretation from that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, I think making fairly basic points which are alluded to in the text, I would have thought already that the Court would be familiar with the claims implied in the first of those tables, that Yugoslavia has a very diverse, multi-ethnic population and certainly did at the time of that census. That is also true of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, shown in table C(2), which indicates the relative sizes of the population of Croats, Muslims, Serbs, those who describe themselves as Yugoslavs and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see, in 1991, the Muslims are 41 per cent, just over double the size of those declaring themselves as Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Over the page, please. The top table is headed "Yugoslav's Ethnic and Confessional Muslims." Just ensure that we all follow those two terms, please, "ethnic and confessional."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to have the opportunity to clarify this, because once again the Court will already be familiar with the reference to a large proportion of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina as Muslims, and normally when one talks about ethnic Muslims, this refers to people who, in the censuses, have been prepared to accept or have offered themselves the designation "Muslim" to describe their national identity. Islam is, of course, a faith, and a large number of other people living in former Yugoslavia were Muslims in that confessional sense, although they would not have responded to the census question, "What is your nationality," by putting down, "Muslim." In that table, C(3), the larger part of former Yugoslavia's Albanian population, there are certain proportions of Catholics principally in Kosovo. The greater proportion of them would have described themselves as Muslims if pressed to give some kind of indication of their confessional identity. The Romi, also gypsies, are not entirely Muslim in their religious adherence. A large proportion of them are. Quite a number are also Orthodox in different parts of former Yugoslavia. Of course, the vast majority of those who would accept the ethnic designation Turks also have some kind of association with Islam, even if it's only a fairly sentimental and historical one, so that the purpose of that first table there, C(3), was to suggest the significance of the, I suppose, the cultural importance of Islam within Yugoslavia, going simply beyond those who would have described themselves as Muslim in the census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And being something that, according to what was declared in the census, was growing in relation to ethnic Muslims between 1971 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, so far as Albanians are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, so far as Romi or gypsies are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. It's interesting to note you've drawn attention to the changing numbers here. I think there is considerable controversy among demographers as to what the causes of those changes might be, because in part, of course, these changes can be attributed to different birth rates, but also in different areas of the country there are good reasons of one kind or another for people to wish to assimilate to the majority ethnic group in their area. So people do change their own ethnic identification over time, and I think this is one of the reasons for including these two tables here, to suggest that surrounding the ethnic designation "Muslim" in Yugoslavia in particular, there is a considerable amount of ambiguity and, indeed, fluidity over time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom table to which we now turn picks up the global figures from the top and simply reveals the distribution of national and confessional Muslims between the various parts of former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct, and the significance of this, I think, is really quite important as far as this case is concerned because it relates to the question of the structure of the former Yugoslavia in terms of republics, and part of the argument which I develop in my report is that for several of those republics, there is no problem when it comes to identifying the republic with a particular dominant ethnic group who can be considered to be -- whose homeland the republic can be considered to be, so that Slovenes naturally look to Slovenia as their homeland. One of the difficulties facing the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is that although, as that table indicates, more than 1,8 million of the 2,3 million people who identify the ethnic designation "Muslim" lived in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They did not constitute a majority of the population of that republic, so that for the republic to have been regarded as their homeland in the same way as Slovenes might look to Slovenia, Montenegrins to Montenegro, would have been politically extremely contentious, so although practically, because of their numerical predominance within the republic, they had a strong association with the republic. That association had to be qualified for important political reasons which I tried to set out in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we turn then to the last of these tables --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Excuse me. One of the corrections that I submitted suggested that that table had been superseded by others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The next exercise I would like your help with, or almost the last, is with, I think, the plans or the maps which the Chamber has only seen so far in black-and-white form. So bundles, as before, for the Chamber itself, for the Judges, for the Defence, and one for the witness. While they are been distributed, Dr. Allcock, I don't know if you've been shown the device on your right-hand side. That's the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I thought it was an instrument of torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the overhead projector, and you may find that you get used to handling the document yourself rather than go through them swiftly in order. The usher will help you, if appropriate, but if you simply take the first one off, which is Z1668,1, that's the one in your right hand. Lay it on the ELMO. If you look at the screen, you should see the document coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you need to point anything to us, you'll be provided with a pointer, but you point not on the screen, you point at the document on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You deal in your report extensively with questions of dialect and their significance, and therefore I can go through these maps quite swiftly. This map of 1993 shows what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, although the majority of South Slav people speak a related group of dialects, which an attempt was made to codify these as Serbo-Croatian, although there has subsequently been some controversy about that, all closely related to each other, but the point that I'm trying to make is that it's very difficult to identify a language which could quite simply and uncontroversially be thought of as being the Croatian language, because the divisions between the major dialect groups don't correspond easily and simply, uncomplicatedly, either to the pattern of state boundaries in the area nor even to the pattern of ethnic distribution in the area. In this first map here, you've got broadly indicated three groups of dialects which are important in the region. The green area toward the top is known as the Kajkavski dialect or Kajkavian dialect. Each of these dialects, incidentally, is identified, for the sake of convenience on the part of linguists, by the word for "what" which is used by speakers of that dialect, so that "kaj" would be the word used for "what", which would be used in that area, although that is by far from being the only distinction. There are differences of vocabulary and others as well that go on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To take it fairly shortly, there is another dialect which we see predominates in the islands themselves, part of the coastal strip and another area, and that's marked blue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's marked blue, yes. This is the Cakavski dialect, which again has quite strong differences between that and the other two dialect groups. But the majority of people in the area speak the dialect known as Stokavian or Stokavski dialect, which is represented by the brown areas of that map. You'll see that although the area covered by the Republic of Croatia is divided between those three major dialect groups, the Stokavian dialect is shared also with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, I wanted to ask the witness if the people speaking these different dialects can still understand each other. In other words, is there really a major difference? So, if you could help us as to what you mean when you say "a dialect." A dialect in relation to which language?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, they would be largely mutually intelligible, although not completely so. It would be impossible to encounter conversations between speakers of these different dialects who, on occasion, certainly would have difficulty in fully understanding each other. But they are not so different from each other as to be completely unintelligible, so that they can -- this is the basis upon which an attempt was made to construct a Serbo-Croatian dialect, in that all of the dialects in that area are believed by linguists to have sufficient in common for them to be organised, systematised, as a single language, although that point, of course, has been contested subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Allcock. As for the dominant dialect, the Stokavski, is it truly the same throughout this region, which is a mountainous region, and we know that often in mountainous regions, there may be certain specifics here and there, so even within that dominant dialect, are there some specific areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: This is the point of the second map, the one that I've called map 2, that draws attention to what is called the Stokavian dialect groups. Within that predominant brown area on the first map, if I can just change the maps over, the coloured areas here represent simply a refinement of the detail within the brown area indicated on the first map, and you'll see that within that Stokavian group of dialects, there are a group of subdialects. In fact, of course, the situation, if one were a professional linguist, one could probably identify further complexities here, but I'm not a linguist and I don't think it's of sufficient relevance to the Court for the Court to go into that level of detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as we've seen from these two maps, the dialects are no particular respecters of the boundaries between Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct. You'll see, looking at the map which is on the screen in front of you at the moment, that the borders of the dialect groups do not correspond with any precision at all to state borders, and I think the significance of this pattern appears even more clearly if we can move on to the third map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll have to probably select a part of the third map to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right. Well, I think we can do it just with that portion which is on the screen at the moment. This map represents -- it's a rather complicated piece of ethnographic cartography -- represents the distribution of ethnic groups according to the 1981 census. It's produced by the Slovene Statistical Institute, and it's not necessary for us to look in too much detail at this. It's the shear mind-numbing complexity of the pattern which is the relevant datum that I want to put before the Court and the fact that you can't map, with any ease, this distribution of people according to their declared ethnicity onto the pattern of dialects which was indicated in the previous two maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you just, I think, to slow down a little, because you're giving a lot of information, and if the technical booth could very kindly focus on the key at the bottom left-hand corner. First of all, perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: If I just move the position of it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, I think, will help, a little bit further up, because we haven't got this fully translated.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Okay, right. Is that okay there? Fold it. Yes, that's a good idea. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In case anybody wants interpretation of some of these words, and I'm not going to go through all of them, only the principal ones, if we start at the left-hand side, the first block in red reflects what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Montenegrins, followed by Croats, Macedonians, Muslims, Slovenes, Serbs, and then those who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next column?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: These are Albanians, Bulgarians, Czechs, Hungarians, Roma or gypsies, Romanians and Rusins. Then the final column, Slovaks, Italians, Turks, Vlahis, and then those who chose to use some other regional identifier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Inevitably, with such a number of peoples, we've run out of colours, effectively, and there comes a point on the map where distinguishing between the colours is difficult or, in reality, impossible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, the point you make is -- well, are there any areas on this map of simple occupation by a simple group, by a single group?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. If we can restore the original position that I gave it here, there are a few. Certainly, if one looks at the area of Montenegro, that's relatively unproblematic. Large areas of Serbia, Eastern Macedonia there, most of Slovenia is relatively homogeneous in its ethnic population, the Zagolj (phoen) area of Northern Croatia and an area down here of Southern Croatia which lapses over into Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see that to the west of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again this is a map, as you've told us, produced from within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Correct, yes, by the Slovene Statistical Institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again on the basis of what, declared nationality census?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Declared nationality in the 1981 census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, please. I think this is a map that you want included and that was additional to the ones in your report, and you wanted it for a small point only. But tell us, please, of 164,3.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right. Yes, this is an interesting map for the following reason: It contains --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right. This is from the same source as the first two maps of dialect areas. It comes from the official Croatian atlas, but the atlas I've used in my original report is of the 1993 edition. The slide which you have in front of you at the moment is of the previous edition, the 1992 edition, and it shows the same information as would have been contained on those earlier maps of dialect groups in Croatia. Now, the reason for my drawing this to the attention of the Court is that the information here relates specifically and exclusively to the Republic of Croatia. Now, in my report, I do make the point, referring to a scholar from the University of Zagreb, Dr. Agocic, who has shown the way in which the representation of Croatia in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina has changed over time, particularly in schoolbooks, so that by implication at least, the claims of the Republic of Croatia on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina become stronger over time. I thought this was a remarkably vivid indication of that kind of thing. But in 1992, we have the official Croatian atlas confining its attention to the Republic of Croatia. In 1993, we have a subsequent edition of that same atlas at least by implication suggesting that socially and culturally, there is a continuity between what has happened in the Republic of Croatia and what's happening in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so at the very least you could say that it's being claimed that Croatia has a legitimate interest of some kind or another in what goes on in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next map, please, 1668,4. This relates to ancient kingdoms and empires. The Chamber has already heard something about this and we may be only marginally concerned, so deal with it very swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think that you probably are largely familiar with this information. I'm not quite sure what Professor Donia presented you with before, but again it refers to the same kind of problem of the difficulties of separating historical claims for territory, particularly when one is looking, so far as we are concerned at the moment, at the relationship between Croatia and any Bosnian state. In the left-hand of those maps here, it is not transmitting very well at the moment, but the area to which I'm pointing at the moment would be the area occupied by the medieval state of Croatia at its greatest extent. It's interesting to compare this, in particular, with the area indicated on the right-hand map, which is the Empire of King Tvrtko to whom Bosnians traced the history of their state. You will see that there's a very substantial overlap between the two areas indicated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next map, please, 1668.5. Again, I think with this we are familiar. There might be little or nothing that you want to add, this being the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: This indicates the area covered in the late 1930s by the Banovina Hrvatska, the attempt to draw together the parts of the first Yugoslavia which were inhabited by a majority of ethnic Croats into a single political unit. Although the aspirations of different Croatian nationalist groups for the extension of a Croatian state into the area which has been the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina varied quite a lot, the Banovina Hrvatska provides one of those historical legitimations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think those who are taking down your every word --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I'm speaking too quickly. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- ask that you breath a little more regularly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I will slow down. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not the speed but the volume.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Is that a better distance for you? Okay. What was the last point? I don't need to repeat that. Okay. That's the significance of that map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next map does need a little explanation and is not necessarily vividly clear, even when the map becomes clear.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: One of the points which I make very strongly in my report is that it's a mistake to look at the problems of the region and, in particular, the causes of armed conflict in the region exclusively in terms of national sentiment and as a result of that. There are very substantial economic issues at stake here, and I quoted at one point in my report or in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to stop you. I was looking at another map, 0081 -- I beg your pardon, Z7597, as I think this is the one -- this is the Croatian military frontier --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Oh, right, there isn't a copy of that in the sheaf that I've been given, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon. The two pages were stuck together when I moved them. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. A small point on this one, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is a relatively small point and it's one which the Court has probably encountered before. There's a tendency to look at ethnic minorities in all of the states of the region as if they are relatively recent interlopers, and I would simply like to emphasise the antiquity of some of these settlements. A great deal can be made of that point. I simply wanted to draw attention here to the fact that from the seventeenth century onwards, large numbers of Orthodox, who subsequently came to identify themselves as Serbs, were settled by the Austro-Hungary Empire in the military frontier region running along the north and northwest areas of what is now Bosnia. This is the basis of subsequent Serbian settlement, and the point of the right-hand map is to show that this is still, to some extent, visible in those areas which subsequently attempted to secede from the Republic of Croatia as autonomous Serbian krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not immediately apparent where the match of shaded areas is from --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the maps are not to an identical scale here, and I haven't had the opportunity to ask a cartographer to superimpose them. I wouldn't claim that there is a complete correspondence between those areas, just that there is a measure of correspondence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what degree are those areas now wholly Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, that remains to be seen. Since the famous Operation Storm in which the Republic of Croatia reasserted its authority over Serbian secessionist forces in that area, I don't know of any systematic attempt to survey the population, but the majority of the Serb population certainly has left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next map, Z1668.7.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right. We're back on target again now. A point which I've tried to make very strongly in my report is that you can't understand the development of the conflict in this area exclusively in terms of the expression of national sentiment or nationalism, that very substantial economic interests underlie the conflict, and, indeed, I refer at one point to a quotation by Franjo Tudjman that Croatia is something of an economic nonsense without placing it alongside with Bosnia. What I've tried to do is to indicate on this map that if you want to communicate between significant areas of Croatia, the cheapest, shortest way of doing so over land is to travel through Bosnia and Herzegovina. So that if you want to go from Osijek to Dubrovnik without an extremely long and dubious detour, you need to go through Bosnia. The principal railway lines between Croatia, between the eastern and western parts of Croatia, run through important railway junctions, such as Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that the red lines are not --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Are a rather sterilised version of those two indication routes. They are not traced from a map. They are simply drawn to indicate the broad lines of the major routes of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, apart from the communication factor, are there any other economic factors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: There certainly are, and these are illustrated on the next map, if I may move on to that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: This may not be immediately very clear, but I think the idea is a very straightforward one, and the area contained within the triangle in the middle is the area of Central Bosnia, and you'll see that Sarajevo is at that point of the triangle, Jajce is up here, and, well, Mostar is down there. So this is the Neretva Valley running here. The point that I'm trying to indicate is that a very significant proportion of Bosnia's economic resources are located within that triangle, in terms of manufacturing capacity, of mining resources, and of power generation resources, as well as important communication routes. So that whoever controls that triangle of territory, in effect, has control over the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that if we're trying to understand what was the point of a struggle for the control of Central Bosnia, it hasn't just to do with the fact that some groups of people might be assumed to have prejudices about other groups of people; it has to do with states, proto states or putative states attempting to control resources which are going to be of major importance to their survival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the black arrows are again the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Just a sketchy indication of the main communication routes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, 1668.9, and I'm dealing with it simply because this is the order in which they turn up in the original report before turning to maps that are additional to those in the report, is a map from Valenta's book --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- proposing movement of peoples in huge numbers. Comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I think that it is the figures, as much as the map, which are of relevance here, and what the map, in fact, shows is that Anto Valenta presupposes a three-stage reorganisation of the distribution of the population of the republic. In the first of these stages, represented by the top pair of arrows, he's suggesting that there could be some kind of exchange of 98.000 Croats from the eastern area and 98.000 Serbs from the second. The second stage, represented by the pair of arrows here (indicating) suggests an exchange of 170.000 Muslims for 170.000 Croats. The third set of arrows there suggests an exchange of 194.000 Serbs for 194.000 Muslims. We've passed over those numbers very quickly, but I'd invite the Court to consider the human consequences of population exchanges on that kind of scale which are treated here rather glibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The publication of this book being when in relation to the war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I haven't got that date in front of me now. I think it's something like 1993, but I'd have to check that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we come to the last map. The last map, which appears in the appendix of your report, is 1668.1 and is the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The significance for the sociologist being?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I'm sure this is a map with which the Court is already thoroughly familiar. The point of it in relation to my report is really to draw attention to the timing and the development of conflict. But area 10 here was one which the Vance-Owen Plan designated as principally an area of Croat control, although looking back at the map of ethnic distribution that I have presented earlier, it would be clear that this is one of the most thoroughly mixed areas of population from before the war and that the designation of this area as being part of a Croat canton can be looked at as one of the stimuli which led to the intensification of war in that area as Croatian forces attempted to consolidate their hold over the area, assuming that this was going to be awarded to them, strengthening their claim in subsequent negotiations internationally, that this, indeed, would be part of a Croat state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I turn now to the additional maps, please, and start off at 1668.11.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute. Give people a chance to take a breath.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The source of these maps appears in the right-hand side about a third of the way down. What is the source?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: The source of these maps, as I understand it, is the Croatian Statistical Office, the official republic's statistics office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This map, the first one, is the area to the south of Zenica. The circles, coloured circles, are well explained by the key at the top, and although there is difficulty in discriminating between green for the Muslims, purple or whatever the colour is for the Yugoslavs, and what looks like black for the others, is that difficulty in discrimination on the colours that we have likely to be significant or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No. In fact, I think it's probably only necessary at this point first to look at one of these maps as an illustration of the idea in general, which the map in front of us will do at the moment, which is of the Busovaca municipality, and it does make the point that you really do need to look at the local level when coming to understand the problems of the pattern of ethnic settlement. It's all very well to look in the statistical handbook and find that the municipality of Busovaca has an ethnic composition of such and such proportion of different groups. But the local complexity of the relationship between different groups is much more considerable than that simple observation would lead us to understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These circles here, as you understand it, when they are read, reflects what for the particular village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: These are local villages. I believe that each of the circles represents a mjesna zajednica, a local neighbourhood. As you pointed out, the red circles represent those localities which had a majority Muslim settlement. I don't think there are significant numbers of Yugoslavs or even Serbs in the area. So that the darker ones represent localities of majority Croat settlement, the open circles, those in which there was no clearly identifiable majority of one ethnic group or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see in Katici, purple, which would appear to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: If I can find it, that seems to be almost the only predominantly Serb settlement in that particular municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Podjele.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can simply turn over to see that we have similar maps for Gornji Vakuf, Jajce, Novi Travnik --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I would make exactly the same points in relation to these other maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There may have been a misinterpretation or a slip of the tongue. Red is for Croat, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Did I say something else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may have done.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you did, I missed it as well. Thank you very much. I want to turn, quite shortly really, to your conclusions and to one or two other matters seeking elaboration only to a limited extent. The Chamber has been provided, in advance of your most recent attendance here, with a summary that you've seen, I think?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the Chamber has that, page 2, paragraph 6, your conclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is there a copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There certainly should be a copy for the interpreters, and it's my fault if one hasn't been provided. My apologies to the interpreters for that oversight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've expressed the view that ethnic cleansing has not occurred spontaneously at the grass roots but has been top down. Just a word or so to amplify that and the materials on which you rely to say that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's quite an important point to establish in relation to understanding what happened in the former Yugoslavia the way in which, certainly in Britain, events were covered in the press, suggested that antagonisms between ethnic groups in the area was something which emerged spontaneously as a result of, Mr. Major's phrase, "ancient hatreds between ethnic groups." I think that what I am doing in my report here is simply summarising the consensus of social scientific colleagues that this is absolutely not the case, that although different ethnic groups had a clear awareness very often of their own identity, that although they were aware of other people's identities, and although a measure of social distance sometimes existed between them which might be reflected in their different patterns of residence, you could not deduce from these that there was a long history of mutual hatred between the groups in question. This is the point of my having introduced the film produced by the anthropologist Tone Bringa which demonstrates a pattern of very amicable relationships between the population of a mixed Muslim and Croat village. So if we're trying to explain why Yugoslavia should have broken down in violence, we can't resort to that as the primary factor of explanation. We have to look elsewhere. A good part of my report has been concerned to point towards other factors, including the circumstances of the break-up of the League of Communists, economic problems of one kind another, we can pursue those if you like, but there are those external and systemic factors which are much more important in accounting for the violent break-up of the state than any notion of diffuse ethnic hostility between the members of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will turn very briefly to those other topics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, but just a clarification. I think that point was also made by Dr. Donia, but even if the ethnic cleansing was orchestrated from the top and filtered down, doesn't it reveal something as to the strength of a sort of undercurrent, that it was caught on so quickly by the masses because they followed the leadership.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think the longer I look at the history of this particular problem, the more I'm persuaded that it's very important to be aware of local differences. We tend to talk about ethnic cleansing as if it's a simple and single phenomenon, as if we know immediately what that means, but, in fact, what we're referring to here is a wide range of very diverse phenomena. Sometimes we're simply dealing with people who are fleeing from the disruption and danger of a war between two armies, so that the displacement of population is incidental to what has been happening. The mechanisms for ethnic cleansing are also quite diverse. I was speaking, not long ago, to a very experienced Slovene journalist friend of mine who is familiar with the area of eastern Bosnia and saying that when she had been visiting that area, talking to people who had been involved, who had been victims of ethnic cleansing, what often happened was that paramilitary forces would come to the village and say to some of the locals, "You will go to your neighbours and you will tell them that if they don't leave, they will be killed, and if you do not tell them that, you will be killed." So that the locals were very often brought into the process of ethnic cleansing under compulsion rather than reflecting their own animosities. I'm not denying that on some occasions and in some localities opportunities of this kind may not have been seized on fairly positively by locals to settle old scores, but we're dealing with a very complicated process here, the causes of which are not always identical in different areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Dr. Allcock, your thesis, which was also presented by Dr. Donia, though not in the same way, is to say that the conflict did not have, as its source, hatred or confrontation among ethnic groups, this ethnic hatred and confrontation being more the result of the conflict rather than being at the origin of the conflict. It was rather the consequence which promoted this hatred and confrontation among ethnic groups and also so that these should not be considered the root causes of the conflict. That is your thesis. But you tell us that there was a considerable differentiation, distinction, between various ethnic groups and identities among those populations. Then came the communist system, and this system, established after the Second World War, did it not freeze, if we could use that term, these ethnic and national differences which broke out again after the system collapsed in the 1990s or at the end of the decade of the 1980s? Couldn't it be said that this did exist, after all, like lava in a volcano which, at a given moment, erupts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I would quarrel with your metaphor, and there are two main points that I would want to make in response to your question here. First of all, I don't deny in my report, indeed I make a feature of the fact, that the sources for mutual suspicion between different ethnic groups are historically available, but they are not permanently present in people's minds and permanent influences upon their behaviour. They need to be triggered by a particular stimuli. If I can just use an illustration, which I don't use in the report, from my own experience when we were children in East Leicester, we used to play the usual chasing games that children play in the school yard, only the contending parties were Highlanders and Redcoats, referring back to the Scottish rebellion of 1745. this does not mean that the children in East Leicester in the 1950s went around hating --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I will slow down. This doesn't mean that you can assume that English children were living in a permanent state of hatred against the Scots. It simply means that every ethnic group has, what I have called in the report, an encyclopaedia of symbols or images about relevant others which may be drawn upon under the appropriate historical circumstances as justifications for particular sorts of action towards them. The other point that I would want to make in response to your question is to challenge what you're saying about the importance of the communist regime. You used the notion of containing historical hatreds which then, in your metaphor, burst out like volcanic lava. The point which I tried to develop in my report is that the way the communist state operated in post-1945 Yugoslavia, it shouldn't be looked at as something which acted to minimise or conceal or contain a sense of ethnic difference, but, indeed, that particular political system, in many respects, created and was responsible for the shape of people's perception of ethnic differences and ethnic relationships in post-1945 Yugoslavia. It was the communist regime which set up the very structure of republics. It was their attempt to deal ideological with the question of nationality which promoted a sense of Muslim identity in the sense of there being a nation. A very important part of the consequence of both communist economic policy and its failure was the intensification of economic conflict between republics, providing the raw materials, in many cases, for the representation of political differences in terms of ethnic differences. So far from being a factor which contained, concealed, or reduced the potential for ethnic conflict in post-war Yugoslavia, I would argue that the communist regime was very important in giving form to and, in some cases, even stimulating the development of ethnic conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one more point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One more question. Have you presented in your report any evidence to support your claim as to what I might call an imposed ethnic cleansing, that is, the leadership saying to the masses, "Go to your neighbour's house and do so and so or you will be killed." Do you have evidence of that? Because it seems to me to be very important if the conflict did not arise out of the history of mutual distrust.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I wasn't requested to deal with that level of detail in my report, so I didn't deal with it in my report. I covered two main areas: One was the question of the development of ethnic identity, the character of ethnic identity in the region, and then the second part of the report to deal more generally with the characteristics of both the Croatian and the Bosnian states. I wasn't asked by the trial team to provide evidence of the sort to which you've referred, so I didn't do so in my report. I assumed that other witnesses would be contributing to those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Robinson's question is do you, in fact, have evidence of that, beyond the particular item you've already given us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, incidentally, yes, I've mentioned the conversation that I've had. But also while preparing and discussing my report with the trial team, I have been given access to a certain amount of documentary material in the archive of the Tribunal, and it does seem to me, from that material, that there is a fair degree of evidence that would support that. But I haven't introduced that in any systematic sense into my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can return to both Judge Robinson, on your right, and Judge Bennouna's first questions and ask you a question that may be susceptible to quite a short answer, was there or is there underlying the peoples of this region a propensity to inter-ethnic violence different from, greater than or lesser than, that which you would find in other multi-ethnic communities around the world?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It's a very broad question, indeed. I wouldn't have said -- if I can answer, since you asked for a brief answer, I would not say that the area of Central Bosnia was distinguished as being particularly prone to ethnic conflict in relation to other areas of which I'm aware, if that's what your question meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that probably is what I meant, although I expressed it differently to try and reflect what I believed was underlying the two Judges' questions. Perhaps we can move on, coming back to that, if it's going to be appropriate, later. I'm going to stick with the document I have, you don't have it in front of you at the moment, and I'm asked by the interpreters to ensure that both of us, when we're having exchanges, leave a gap between the question and the answer. So don't --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I do apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be the first time you've given evidence in this way or, indeed, given evidence orally at all.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's move on. You've already dealt, 6(B), this is, for those following the document, with the fact that Bosnia was unique in the former Yugoslavia because it was not the homeland of any single ethnic group. You've also, I think, dealt already with the International Community's efforts serving to reinforce ethnic divisions. That's the Vance-Owen Plan, in particular?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is part of the material conclusions that lead to your wider conclusion that the inter-ethnic conflict was caused by a breakdown in political and economic foundations of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: A part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything additional that you wish particularly to highlight, and you can do it in summary form, that leads to that conclusion at the moment? If not, we'll move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Nothing immediately comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, to round off this area, as you are going on to another question, I remember the answer of the expert, Dr. Allcock, that the communist regime stimulated the development of ethnic conflict, because it did not contain these things. How come then that during that regime, the regime under President Tito in Yugoslavia, the conflict did not explode? As far as we know, there were no explosions of violence. How was it possible that those relations were contained and remained peaceful? Your conclusion may appear to be rather paradoxical in relation to this period between 1945 and 1985 or 1990.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think you've slightly placed a stronger interpretation on what I said than I would have intended when you talked about the communist regime containing the propensity to violence or the communist regime stimulating ethnic conflict. What I said was that the communist regime operated to stimulate people's sense of ethnic identity and their awareness of this, and the social and political significance of that perhaps of ethnic identity. But I wouldn't like to suggest that throughout the post-1945 period, Yugoslavia was necessarily a seething hotbed of ethnic violence or potential ethnic violence. Sometimes, in some occasions, problems of ethnic conflict did become quite serious, in Croatia itself, for example, between 1971, 1972, in Kosovo on several occasions, but you shouldn't form the impression that the communist authorities were faced with a constant struggle to repress ethnic conflict. That's not my impression at all, if I've understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The stimulation of ethnic identity was inter alia by either creation or recreation of the constituent states along ethnic lines, as opposed to, for example, creating fresh banovinas which transected ethnic, an experiment that had been tried and failed decades before.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. The structure of Yugoslav politics was cast in terms of a pattern of relationships and subsequently conflicts between republics. So that if the major political conflicts which are driving the political process along are conflicts between republics which are largely identified with ethnic groups of one kind or another, the sense of ethnic identity and its relevance to political conflict is enhanced in that process. The motor of political development and political conflict is the conflict between republics which then draws with it, as a consequence, a heightened sense of people's ethnic awareness and its relevance for politics. So that when the Yugoslav state breaks up, you have then the formation of ethnic parties, and the stories carried on in those terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next conclusion was that the new Croat leadership adopted policies and practices uniting the Croatian people, and you build that, in part, on the HDZ's partial rehabilitation of the independent state of Croatia, but you're very careful, I think, in your comments at page 61 to 62 to qualify that. Just in a sentence, how partial was partial or how near to complete was this rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It was very partial. The HDZ is an interesting phenomenon in that it was, in effect, a coalition of people who had sometimes quite different views about the nature of Croatia and the future of a Croatian state, so that it may be possible to find within that party people who had quite strongly different views. The relevance of the independent state of Croatia was that the HDZ tried to build its claim for there being an independent Croatia, built on the debris of Yugoslavia, on the notion of the historical continuity of a Croatian state going back to the Middle Ages. They, therefore, were compelled to rely, to some extent, on the NDH in saying that this was also a legitimate bearer of that tradition of independent Croatian statehood. I certainly wouldn't want it to be thought that the HDZ took over all of the ideological baggage of its predecessors in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under B, we have summarised, or it has been summarised from your report, that the HDZ programme created the impression that Serbs in Croatia were alien and hostile, that they feared being reduced to second class citizens, and the HDZ's actions set a precedent for ethnic exclusivism that was to follow?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that simple conclusion is one you still hold?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fearing the creation of an independent Bosnia would make the Croats living there politically insignificant. Your view is that the HDZ had that fear and claimed that the BiH government aimed to create an Islamic state, raising Croats' fears.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. There is a parallelism between the fears of Serbs in Croatia that they would be reduced to second class citizenship by the creation of a Croatian state and the fears of Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they would similarly be marginised, since only about 18 per cent of the population of the republic were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we divert from the printed text for one question that I wanted to deal with? At the time of the creation of Herceg-Bosna, and Herceg-Bosna so long as it existed, to what extent did that body have the qualities of either a nation or a state?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I don't think that you could talk about Herceg-Bosna in terms of a nation, because one of the things which is very clear about the material that I've seen published in relation to Herceg-Bosna is that they insisted on their Croatian identity, that they were part of the Croatian nation and not a different nation. But certainly speaking sociologically, there's no doubt in my mind that the project of Herceg-Bosna was to set up a state. The way a sociologist would approach the nature of a state would be to talk about the monopoly of the legitimate use of force over a given territory, and when you have established an institution such as the HVO, effectively an army, you have got the creation of a civil service which is intending to administer political affairs in that state, the Croatian judiciary and educational system, it seems to me to be pretty unambiguous that the project of Herceg-Bosna was to set up a state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we turn to the part of the HDZ BiH programme, which was to challenge the sovereignty of the recognised government. You summarise the position of Franjo Tudjman. We've heard that elsewhere and needn't dwell on it. You say that the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia provided an incentive for both the Croats and the Serbs to seek partition, joining with, in each case, their larger neighbouring nation states, and that to this end Tudjman and the HDZ aided the local HDZ BiH that opposed the multi-ethnic and united Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything you need to add to that, or can we move on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, only that the evidence in support of that seems to have been growing steadily, and if we need to, I can talk about that further. But you have suggested that we need to move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, the organisation and implementation of this programme, you say, remained in the hands of leading figures. Just one thing. Before you became involved in this particular case, did you know the name "Kordic" at all or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, I hadn't encountered him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Kostroman"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, I had encountered that name. If you look at the list of publications which I've put in my little author note there, you'll see that there are two reports which I wrote on the creation of new political parties in, first of all, former Yugoslavia and then its successive states, and the name "Kostroman," I recall, had cropped up in one of those volumes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But perhaps just a word or so more about the last conclusion that we've cited in the very short summary, to the effect that the model of management which mixed military and civilian spheres of responsibility was used in the Second World War by the Communist Party of Yugoslavia and was adopted by the HDZ. Can you give us just one or two of the characteristics of that sort of management, including, in particular, dealing with rotation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. One of the interesting features of the political order which the parties attempted to set up even before the end of the Second World War was the use of members of the party, party cadres, to infuse both the supposedly civilian administration and to effectively ensure political control of the military, so that you had a very blurred set of boundaries between what was the party, what was administration, and what was the military. One of the curious things about not only the situation in the HVO but it was a tendency that had been remarked on in Yugoslavia throughout the late '70s was a tendency to revert rather more to that kind of pattern of fluidity. The 1974 constitution insisted upon there being rotation between various leadership positions in all aspects of economic and political life and tended to promote throughout the whole Yugoslavia, not simply Croatia, a sense of fluidity and ambiguity about where the borders of one set of institutions ended and the others began, and I was just struck by the similarities between those systems and the way in which the structures of Herceg-Bosna seemed to operate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just developing that by one further question, centralisation and the presidency within these structures, is there anything you would like to add on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, I think I've made these points fairly fully in my report. But, yes, in relation to the Republic of Croatia, one of the things which has been remarkable about the post-Communist pattern of politics in Croatia is a very pronounced tendency towards centralisation around the power of a presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge enough to comment on the similarities or dissimilarities between that and Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: The detailed knowledge I have of the operation of Herceg-Bosna wouldn't run to a detailed analysis of that kind of thing, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you deal with -- well, whether you deal in your report or not with religious symbols and so on, can you just look at this exhibit, please, which is in the core documents and is Prosecution Exhibit 321? I have copies available, in any event. Now, this is, I think, Dr. Allcock, a document you've only seen very recently.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Waved under my nose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I hope you've had a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have had a chance to read it, do you have any comment that you wish to make about it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there's a dimension of developments here which interests me greatly as a sociologist, and that refers to the extent to which populations might be considered to be under pressure in relation to other groups of people. We tend to rather concentrate on the presence or absence of a physical threat, and the whole discussion of ethnic cleansing has tended to concentrate very much on the threat of armed reprisals, that kind of thing. As a sociologist, I'm impressed by the importance of symbols and the bearing of symbols on the development of political action, and the way in which you can persuade people pretty emphatically to do what you want to do or to change their perception of themselves in relation to you without resorting to force. I referred to this in a limited way in my report by talking about, for example, the referendum on independence in Croatia, when voters were led in processions in Zade (phoen) by the town Ban. It makes participation in voting in a certain way part of a kind of a public festival. The negative side of that is you can surround other people with symbols of your own dominance as a group within the community and, conversely, you can make sure the symbols of your own identity and its significance and its value for the culture as a whole are minimised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you just for this purpose: Can you lay that document on the overhead projector, so that although we haven't gone through it in detail, what you're talking about can be understood by anyone following the trial? In summary, it's an order dealing with religious symbols of the Catholic faith made in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right. So that I would expect that the consequence of this kind of order, if it was in fact implemented, would be really quite considerable on a population who would not consider themselves to be Catholics, that in every public place there are now present images of the importance, the power, the significance of a Catholic community. And the converse, of course, of this would be the minimisation and exclusion, the reduction of the presence of symbols of any other community who are not Catholic. The French sociologist, Pierre Bourdieu, has been responsible for the creation in recent years of a theory of what he calls symbolic violence, and I think this is a very clear illustration of symbolic violence. In order to perpetrate violence on other people, you don't necessarily have to go and hit them or shoot them. The effect can be just as dramatic, just as impelling, if you apply to them symbolic means of coercion, and this seems to me to be a dramatic illustration of Pierre Bourdieu's theory of symbolic violence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Flags, may they also have an effect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: They can do, yes, and either the omnipresence of certain flags or corresponding, and this is very common elsewhere in Yugoslavia, the prohibition upon the use of your own flag, which is usually the other side of the same coin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The remaining conclusions set out in your report, are they conclusions you still adopt?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I've not changed my position with respect to any of the items in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that report be given exhibit number 1668. Thank you very much. You'll be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have a question to Dr. Allcock. Still regarding the question that I put a moment ago regarding the role of the Communist system, regarding the strengthening of ethnic identity, you did nevertheless say somewhere in your report that the Muslims were frustrated, in a sense, during that regime because they were the only ones, while their ethnicity was being strengthened, they didn't have the right to a state. What did you mean when you said that they never considered Bosnia as a state? I'm quoting you from page 23. (In English) " In the specific case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, however, the system actively promoted the ethnogenesis of 'Muslims,' while denying the legitimacy of any aspirations which they may have developed for the political embodiment of that identity in a state."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Muslims were not the only group to feel frustrated in that sense, and I think looking at the contemporary situation, you would say that Albanians in Kosovo had the same sort of experience. The reason why I commented in particular on the sense of frustration of Bosnians was that they were in an ambiguous situation. They were referred to as a narod, as a nation, as one of the charter groups of a South Slav state, and yet it was unclear, given the structure of politics within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they did have the same dignity as others who were supposedly given that status of narod. They were in an ambiguous situation there, and I think that is the focus of my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Why was this reserved for the Muslims within ex-Yugoslavia and not to other ethnic groups? Why was this fate reserved for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think in large measure because of the structural population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It certainly shouldn't be looked at, if this is the tenor of your questions, as some kind of hostile position on the part of the regime towards Muslims. In many respects, the Yugoslav Communist regime could be seen as having a very positive attitude towards Islam. Many of the leading states within the non-align movement were also Muslim states, and some critics of the Yugoslav nationalities policy have suggested that this attribution of a state of a nation to Muslims in Yugoslavia in some sense could have been seen as favouring them, you know, and attempting to curry favour with other leading states within the non-align movement. It certainly shouldn't be looked at as any attempt to deliberately disprivilege them, but they were faced with this embarrassing problem, that you can't really make Bosnia-Herzegovina the homeland of Muslims, because to make that suggestion does carry the implication that somehow or another they have some kind of particular relationship to the state which Serbs and Croats. And there is certainly a very large proportion of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina which have not only a large representation in the population but very strong historical connections with the region as well. It's a very delicate balancing game here as to what symbolic importance you give to nationality and how you represent the role of nationality within the political life of the community. It's an attempt of the Communist authorities to square the circle, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, cross-examination. Who is representing the Defence? Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to begin your cross-examination today or do you want to deal with it altogether? We have got another hour or so remaining. Can you usefully use it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm in the Court's hands, to quote from my colleague. I can use some of it, I can use half an hour, 45 minutes of it, certainly, and perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it might be sensible, since time is short, if we adjourn now for a quarter of an hour and then you have half an hour or so to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Dr. Allcock, my name is Bob Stein. I represent Dario Kordic. Cross-examined by Mr. Stein:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I first ask, sir, in what year you got your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I got the Ph.D. I think it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And its title?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I forget the exact title, but it was actually the study of tourism in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to help you. "Studies in the sociology of tourism, with special reference to the role of tourism in the development of Yugoslav society."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the title.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's described as an essay on constructing tourist identities.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, actually the dissertation was a collection of materials covering a variety of aspects of the nature of tourism in Yugoslav society, its economic and social and political significance, and the notion of tourist identities there refers -- has two references; one, of the consequences for the development of tourism for the way in which Yugoslavs look to themselves and experience their own identities, but also the identity of tourists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it that your research was done during your summers travelling in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
