utterances.text: You're quite wrong about that, no. I'm accustomed to receiving this kind of response to work on tourism, which somehow suggests that to study tourism, one must be a tourist. Actually, tourism has now become one of the largest industries in the world and has an enormous significance both for the economies of the countries concerned, especially the Republic of Croatia, and also for the social lives of people caught up in it. The greater part of my research was done, I suppose, over a period of about eight years, but the nature of the case is that that would be spread over a variety of visits, most of which were in fact made during the winter and not exclusively to tourist resorts. I shouldn't like you to think that I spent my time enjoying myself while pretending to be an academic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there would be nothing wrong with enjoying and studying at the same time, Doctor. Your master's degree, sir, when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I finished that, I think, in 1968.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a degree that you studied for and then took a test?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That was a research degree. Well, a mixture of examination of my course work and by thesis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The title of that thesis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It was the study of the nuclear disarmament movement in Canada.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your current position is where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: The University of Bradford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were hired when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I began to work in Bradford in early October of 1966.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are a lecturer there, as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I am at the moment, although my situation is rather ambiguous. I am actually paid as a senior lecturer, and as we sit here at the moment, a committee is meeting to discuss my promotion. I hope to get good news when I return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So right now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Formally, my position at the moment is lecturer and head of the research unit in southeast European studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not a tenured position, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a tenured position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you teach students?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I have a mixture of things. I have a sort of Jeckyl-and-Hyde existence. By day, the university pays me to teach general sociology to students in the humanities department, and otherwise I come out in a completely different persona as a sociologist studying southeastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bradford actually doesn't have a department of sociology, does it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It doesn't have a dedicated department of sociology, but there are quite a lot of sociologists distributed among the number of different departments. I'm in the humanity department, but we have a management centre in which there are sociologists, a development study centre, plus there is applied social studies. I think there are six or seven departments in which sociologists are represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also fair to say, Doctor, that your research between 1967 and 1988 dealt with issues involving migration?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Agriculture?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tourism, which we've talked about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the perceptions of the Balkans by the foreign traveller?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it you are currently developing your former work in tourism to a study of the problems of dissonant heritage in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, that was a project which I entertained before I became -- was drawn quite so heavily into the study of political affairs, as I have at the moment. I've, unfortunately, definitively had to move away from the study of tourism, unless one considers the specific branch of military tourism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the short answer is, "Yes," but you're not working on it actively?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I'm not working on it actively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is "dissonant heritage"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: The idea of heritage I don't suppose needs explanation to the Court, but our heritage is generally looked at as something of which any particular group of people can be proud. Unfortunately, for a variety of groups of people, including, I'm sure, the English, parts of our heritage are not ambiguous in that respect. They require some sort of special explanation as to how we cope with them, what their symbolic significance is for us, and also how we present those rather embarrassing parts of our heritage, in particular, to visitors. This, I think, is of particular interest in relation to Yugoslavia and has a very direct bearing on the sort of thing we're talking about at the moment, in that there have been some rather unsavoury aspects of Yugoslav history and yet the tourist industry manages to make something of those in presenting the history of the various South Slav peoples to tourists. It's exactly the same problem in another form to which we have already alluded in talking about the problems of the HDZ in dealing with the heritage of the independent State of Croatia during the war; how do you deal with your heritage in a way which can be presented to other people in an acceptable way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I gather from your web site, frankly, that your area of expertise includes the media role in democratisation of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: This is an area I teach to undergraduates. I'm not engaged in research on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You teach that to undergraduates, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Democracy relative to the mass media's role in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, this again -- I'm not quite sure where you're getting this information from, but the work that I do on mass communications, the course which I teach with a colleague to students in the humanities in which we look at a variety of aspects of the sociology of popular culture and mass communication, I do use some materials from southeast Europe in that course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You teach a course on tourism as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is one of your areas of expertise, though?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, but there's some crossover here obviously between these, the reporters, my teaching, and other such interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, you list as areas of expertise political development in the former Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And social change in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What I'm doing is listening to the French at the same time, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The research unit in southeast European studies at the University of Bradford, that's not a department of the university; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It's not a department, no. It's a research unit. It's a grouping of people from different departments who share research interests in the region in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Membership in that unit is open to all staff and graduate students.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Who have relevant areas of interest in the region, correct, and we have some honorary participants as well who are not full-time members of either the staff or the student body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, it's wide-open membership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, it's not wide open, in the sense that we would want to know the people do have a serious research interest in the area and they have a degree of competence in pursuing it. It's not like a bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it, as part of your duties as well, you advise two international organisations who recruit personnel for businesses in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, I have done that and I've advised a number of organisations in the past, but this is not a regular contractual business at all. I was approached at one point by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to advise about the recruitment of their staff. I was approached by the United Nations, when they were establishing the UNPROFOR mission in Zagreb, to advise them about the recruitment of staff also. I was approached by this Tribunal in the early days to advise them. But there's no regular retainer or contractual obligation here. These are just approaches that are made from time to time because the research unit has a reputation of contacts and knowledge in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take the gist of your meaning to be you got a phone call?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, or a letter sometimes. Sometimes the relationship can be rather longer standing than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in these instances, they were relatively short calls and short-standing relations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Of varying lengths of correspondence, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it, sir, that as a sociologist, you feel free to study and to opine on some, if not all, of the following I'm going to mention: Ethnic origins; yes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Man and society?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That covers just about everything, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: You could hardly make any sociological comment or whatever without covering that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: History?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, it depends how you interpret that. I certainly would not see myself as being a professional historian, but you can only view society in a historical sense in terms of its development over time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Political process?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cultural process?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, once again, that's like the man and society thing, isn't it? This is a very general topic, but one would want to know from what particular respect one was pursuing that thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Religion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: From time to time, I've worked on religion, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Linguistics?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, not linguistics. That's a very technical area. Obviously, language is socially significant, is an element of culture, and becomes extremely important, both in political processes and in others, but I certainly wouldn't regard myself as an expert in linguistics, and never have I pretended to either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Race and religious issues -- I'm sorry. Race and racial issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Discuss about race doesn't figure very much in relation to southeastern Europe, so I certainly would not say that any of the work that I've done touches on discussions of race relations in the sense that that's come to be used as a phrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, however, something that sociologists are familiar with and comment on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nationalistic issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Migration?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I've worked on migration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Demography?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: To a very limited extent. It's one of the points I've been trying to make to colleagues, that sociology as a profession has tended to be rather ignorant of demography. So my work on demography has been largely to remind colleagues that we should read the work of others, rather than do any original work in it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Geography?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No. Again, geography is a separate discipline. I certainly wouldn't describe myself as a geographer, nor as having done work in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Psychology?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Again, as a cognate discipline, I think as a social scientist, the borders between different disciplines are rather permeable, and you need to know some things that are going on in other areas. But I would never describe myself as a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you say, you say in your work as a sociologist, there are elements of looking at the discipline of psychology?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Occasionally, I have to read works which are by people who would describe themselves as psychologists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You studied, as we indicated earlier, mass media?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I do some teaching in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Social structure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, that's almost the redefinition of sociology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Social mores --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stein, I don't think we are being helped by this very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I think, Mr. Stein, if I may make a suggestion, that in order to gain time, it would be better to ask Dr. Allcock whether he is a generalist or whether he specialises in sociology. Because in all spheres of science, there are generalists and specialists. So perhaps you could ask him that, and if the answer is the latter, then you can ask what is his speciality. In that way, we could gain time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the Judge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I followed the question, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you answer the Judge's question or shall I recast it for you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, I can answer the question. In the nature of the case as a teacher of undergraduates within the department of humanities, I have to, in many respects, be a generalist, because this is the nature of the curriculum which we teach to undergraduate students. As a specialist, there are very few social scientists working on the affairs of Yugoslavia and its successor states, and, in fact, even fewer sociologists. I think I am the only tenured sociologist in the British higher education system whose primary research interest is in the affairs of Yugoslavia and its successor states. In the nature of the case, I am under considerable pressure to take an interest in a variety of different aspects in the transformation of the Yugoslav society in order to meet the changing nature of interest in the region. But I would remind you also that what you've been doing in your comments is summarising a research career which has extended well over 30 years, so that although you've touched on a wide range of issues relating to Yugoslav society, my interests in those has been particular periods, and I've never attempted the feat of trying to do all of them at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So, Mr. Allcock, you are a generalist.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on my own question, if I may, there's no aspect of the human experience that falls outside of the realm of sociology?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that's a helpful question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: We will talk about that in the bar afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you yourself published yourself any book?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: At the time of writing, I am not the single author of an entire book. I've edited a large number, and there's a very substantial book with the publisher at the moment. But at the moment, I am not the sole author of a book-length study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that the majority of your editing was with regard to issues surrounding tourism?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, that is certainly not true. In fact, the work that I've done on tourism, I believe, doesn't figure very much in the report that I've given here. The work which I was involved in editing, for example, on Yugoslavia's defence and security issues was a major study there, the work which I did on Yugoslavia in transition did nothing -- well, it involved one chapter on tourism. So, no, most of my work, I would say, has not been on tourism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your opinion in this case has not been put out for peer review or the general public?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your opinion in this case has not been put out for peer review or in the general public?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Are you talking about the report which I've presented to the Court here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, in the nature of the case, that is so, because I understood I was writing a report of a confidential character for the Court. I thought it would be inappropriate to seek review from other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it also from your resume, sir, that you edit encyclopaedias on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: You should steer clear of the plural. There is a volume of which I am the chief editor, which appeared at the end of last year, co-edited by Marko Milivojovic and John Horton, which is "The Conflict in the Former Yugoslavia: An Encyclopaedia". That is the only one which I have edited. I have contributed to other encyclopaedias, including the Encyclopaedia Britannica, but that is the only one which I've edited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all your work as an editor, an author, or even as a tourist, you've never heard of Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Until I came to work with this Court, I had not encountered the name Dario Kordic. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask, before you did your research, to speak with Mr. Kordic or any member of his counsel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, because the kind of questions which I was asked to -- on which to prepare my report by the Prosecution team dealt principally with aspects of the nature of ethnic identity, the nature of nationality and nationalism within Yugoslavia, and some general considerations about Croatian and Bosnian politics. So the initial point of orientation that I was given was to provide that background material and not an assessment of the career of Dario Kordic. That was not my brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your work in this case, did you read of the Defence submissions to determine whether we covered those issues at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I was shown some material which the Defence had -- your initial brief, yes, I was shown that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you shown that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I made a visit some time ago to The Hague to meet with the Prosecution team, and on that occasion, they allowed me to see that material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, your report, if I read it correctly, has no end notes or annotations or footnotes; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I didn't consider this was appropriate because of two reasons: First of all, I understand that the people likely to read it are under pressure to read a very considerable amount of documentation and, therefore, that in as far as it was possible, I should be relatively brief about this. But, secondly, I didn't think that the report that I was presenting was that kind of document. It was a report and not an academic book. I'm very happy to provide a reading list, if you should wish to pursue these matters further, but I didn't think it was appropriate to provide those kinds of notes on this occasion. It was a deliberate choice on my part not to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your part, you were not instructed to do so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I was not instructed to do so. I was simply asked to write a report, and I decided that the form in which I presented the report would meet what I understood to be the needs of the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, your masters thesis, your Ph.D. thesis, your professional writings contained footnotes, annotations, and end notes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Some of them do. Some of them are in a variety of different forms. My contribution, for example, to the Encyclopaedia Britannica does not contain footnotes because it's not that kind of publication. Every author has to make a judgement about what are the rules of the game in writing a particular sort of publication and what are the needs of the audience in question. So on this occasion, I decided that it was not appropriate to treat this as an academic publication in that standard sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you this: Do you belong either to the British Sociological Association or to the American Sociological Association?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: To the British Sociological Association and the International Sociological Association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before I go on to something else, I want to deal right up front with this exhibit, which is Z321, the one that was thrust in front of you. May we put it on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who thrust this in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It was given to me by members of the Prosecution team. I think the person whose hands actually bore it were -- I've suddenly had a blank here -- the lady sitting in the middle there. I've forgotten her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Ms. Somers. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She handed it to you; she didn't thrust it to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: She offered it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good. You note that that document is dated 16 December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to have a degree in sociology to know that's the Christmas season?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you note with care paragraph 3: "Religious symbols are to be returned to places where they formally stood, and we must be wise in implementing global Croatian policy and must not irritate anyone with our actions. This order is to be carried out in a subtle and systematic way."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand your direct testimony, you're unaware as to how this order was carried out on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's true. All I've had in front of me is this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to whether or not it was carried out in a subtle way or not, you have no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, but what I was commenting on in my direct testimony is the -- I think you have to place this sort of action within the political and social context in which it stood, in which people had already been rather anxious about these kinds of things, and the potential for causing offence was really rather considerable. I'm not aware that the -- I'm certainly not aware, as you've suggested, as to what the actual implementation of the policy might have been, but it does seem to me to be an extraordinarily risky thing, to go around placing, publicly, symbols of one's national and religious identity in an area of mixed ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even around Christmastime?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BARTLETT ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I think one has to be cautious about these kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect, I promised you roughly half an hour, and that's where I am, and with your permission, I would defer the rest of our examination until a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate you're going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Be in my deferral or be in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When we have him back, I expect to be two hours or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, will you be cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would appreciate if we can continue after them, which is our original plan. Only if you insist, we may, but then we will be probably wasting some time. We wouldn't be productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll be less time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Less, certainly. An hour or so max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We'll adjourn the cross-examination. Dr. Allcock, I hope you've been told that you're going to have to come back. I'm sorry about that, but it looks as though it's the only way in which the cross-examination can be concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I hope that a convenient date can be found for you. It is the practice here to tell witnesses not to talk to anybody about their evidence, and I, of course, repeat that to you during this adjournment, and that does include members of the Prosecution. But, of course, you can talk to them about your arrangements for coming back. It's mainly about your evidence. If you would like to go now and be back, please, when it's convenient and when it's arranged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if a convenient date can be arranged, the sooner the better, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand from what's been said, that half a day is required, effectively, possibly a little more. As the Defence know from a letter they received and that I hope has now found its way to your corridor, the confidential witness who was to have been taken in a week or so's time is not a witness who can be taken at that time, and so I'm finding other witnesses, and I've listed some, to cover the rest of the available hearing dates between now and the summer break. It's possible that Dr. Allcock may be available in that very last week when I think we have two and a half days. There it is, I'm told I've got that wrong as well. It may therefore be September, I'm afraid, before he can be dealt with finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, are there any other matters you want to raise now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Just for the hearings next week, we are going to amend our hearing times slightly, which we trust will cause no inconvenience. We are going to sit each day from half past 9.00 in the morning until 11.00, then take a slightly longer break than we have been doing, and sit again from 11.30 to 1.00, the normal statutory break at lunchtime until half past 2.00, and then in the afternoon we'll sit from half past 2.00 until 4.15. So we adjourn now until Monday at half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.48 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of July, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
